newsitem.title: INDONESIA: S.E. Asian Cocoa - Prices mixed, Indonesia upbeat.
newsitem.headline: S.E. Asian Cocoa - Prices mixed, Indonesia upbeat.

text.p: Southeast Asian cocoa prices were mixed on Wednesday, with Indonesian values tailing a sharp rise in New York overnight while Malaysian levels were lower on slow demand amid ample stocks, regional traders said.
Indonesian traders said the main crop harvest was producing ample supply in Ujung Pandang, capital of the key growing region of South Sulawesi although rains were affecting quality.

"It has been raining regularly in Ujung Pandang, and some of the beans coming in are moist," one trader said. "But because moist beans fetch lower prices, farmers and middlemen are trying to dry the beans before selling them."
He said the sentiment in Ujung Pandang was bullish, with prices rising in line with gains in New York overnight.
Cocoa was quoted at 2,900-2,950 rupiah a kg in Ujung Pandang, up from 2,850-29,250 rupiah on Tuesday.
Cocoa prices ended sharply higher across-the-board in New York on Tuesday, bolstered by local and currency-linked arbitrage buying, New York dealers said.
Benchmark July futures rose $24 higher a tonne to finish at $1,409, after ranging from $1,418-$1,385. Spot month May ended $25 higher at $1,399.

"Some players who had been buying aggressively seemed to have slowed, but others are continuing to purchase," one trader said, adding that a Malaysian company had been exploring the possibility of opening an office in Ujung Pandang.
"Production in Malaysia is getting smaller, and the company is keen on buying directly from farmers here," he added.
Another trader said cocoa arrivals in Ujung Pandang were comparatively lower, adding that daily arrivals ranged from 400-500 tonnes this week compared with 700-800 tonnes in the same week last year.
"I don't know the reasons behind the decline...whether it is related to weather or to poor care for the trees," he said.
In Malaysia, players said there was still adequate bean stocks in the market to feed the immediate needs of importers and grinders, though short-covering activities were continuing.
Local prices fell this week, despite the rise in New York, and dealers attributed this to technical adjustments.
"Generally, it's been a quiet week," said a trader. "People have enough beans for near-term but the cautious ones are still buying from Indonesia, the Ivory Coast and other places."
Another trader said local bean supply could still not match demand and projections for imports will become clearer by June.

On Wednesday, the Malaysian Cocoa Board quoted Standard Malaysian Cocoa (SMC) Grade 1 A out of Tawau, the country's main growing area, at an average of 3,320 ringgit a tonne, down 50 ringgit from the week before.
The board quoted the SMC 1B grade out of Tawau at an average of 3,270 ringgit, also down 45 ringgit from previously.
Traders offered the SMC 1A at 3,270 ringgit a tonne and the SMC IB at 3,345-3,355 ringgit.
